claim: EMBLEM is a strategy to track cell lineage using endogenous mitochondrial DNA variants in ATAC-seq data.
source: Here we describe EMBLEM, a strategy to track cell lineage using endogenous mitochondrial DNA variants in ATAC-seq data.
evidence: This is the primary description of the method presented in the abstract.

claim: Somatic mutations in mitochondrial DNA can reconstruct cell lineage relationships at single cell resolution with high sensitivity and specificity.
source: We show that somatic mutations in mitochondrial DNA can reconstruct cell lineage relationships at single cell resolution with high sensitivity and specificity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing detection rates and false positive rates.

claim: EMBLEM extends lineage tracing to any eukaryotic organism without genetic engineering.
source: EMBLEM extends lineage tracing to any eukaryotic organism without genetic engineering.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the method and is based on the fact that it uses endogenous mutations.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing of reporter constructs allowed synthetic reconstruction of cell lineage relationships in model organisms.
source: Specifically, genome editing of reporter constructs via CRISPR-Cas9 allowed synthetic reconstruction of cell lineage relationships in model organisms, and has been coupled with transcriptome profiling to inform cell fates (Spanjaard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Prospective 'mutate-and-record' methods cannot be utilized in living humans, archival clinical samples, or any wild type organism.
source: These prospective 'mutate-and-record' methods provide powerful tools to resolve the developmental origin of cells in genetically engineered cells and organisms, but cannot be utilized in living humans, archival clinical samples, or any wild type organism (Woodworth et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a known limitation of existing methods.

claim: Recent advances in sequencing enable naturally occurring somatic mutations to be used as lineage markers.
source: Recent advances in sequencing enable naturally occurring somatic mutations to be used as lineage markers, which usually required single-cell genome sequencing to capture the sparse genetic information (Lee-Six et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ATAC-seq enriches for mtDNA reads compared to whole exome sequencing, low coverage whole genome sequence, or PCR-free, high-coverage whole genome sequence.
source: ATAC-seq enriches for mtDNA reads compared to whole exome sequencing (WES), low coverage whole genome sequence (WGS_L), or PCR-free, high-coverage whole genome sequence (WGS_H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B comparing different sequencing methods.

claim: ATAC-seq enables a 17-fold or greater enrichment of mtDNA compared to exome sequencing or whole genome sequencing in GM12878 human B cells.
source: ATAC-seq enables a 17-fold or greater enrichment of mtDNA compared to exome sequencing or whole genome sequencing in GM12878 human B cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different sequencing methods.

claim: ATAC-seq leads to an average ~18,000X coverage of mtDNA.
source: ATAC-seq enables a 17-fold or greater enrichment of mtDNA compared to exome sequencing or whole genome sequencing in GM12878 human B cells (Figure 1B), leading to an average ~18,000X coverage of mtDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 27 mitochondrial variants were detected from GM12878 cells using ATAC-seq.
source: With this coverage, we detected 27 mitochondrial variants from GM12878 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 13 of the variants detected in GM12878 cells have a variant allele frequency greater than 90%, which are known as homoplasmic variants.
source: 13 of these variants have a variant allele frequency (VAF) greater than 90%, which are known as homoplasmic variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and uses established terminology.

claim: 14 low frequency mitochondrial DNA variants were detected in GM12878 cells, with VAFs ranging from 0.1% to 24%.
source: We also detected 14 low frequency mitochondrial DNA variants, with VAFs ranging from 0.1% to 24% (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: mtDNA is not chromatinized and is therefore highly accessible.
source: ATAC-seq effectively enriches for mtDNA. While mtDNA is present in many kinds of DNA sequence libraries, it is substantially enriched in ATAC-seq libraries due to the fact that mtDNA is not chromatinized and is therefore highly accessible
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial DNA structure.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA is a ~ 16 kb circular genome with ~10 fold higher mutation rate compared to the nuclear genome.
source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a ~ 16 kb circular genome with ~10 fold higher mutation rate compared to the nuclear genome.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial DNA characteristics.

claim: mtDNA incrementally accumulates unique, irreversible genetic mutations that are passed on to daughter cells even in healthy humans.
source: Hence, mtDNA incrementally accumulates unique, irreversible genetic mutations that are passed on to daughter cells even in healthy humans and may be used for lineage tracing (Morris et al., 2017), (Fellous et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of somatic mtDNA mutations are noncoding and thought to be passenger.
source: The majority of somatic mtDNA mutations are noncoding and thought to be passenger (Ju et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The number of mitochondria (and therefore mtDNA) range from several hundreds to >10,000 per cell in different cell types.
source: Importantly, the number of mitochondria (and therefore mtDNA) range from several hundreds to >10,000 per cell in different cell types, facilitating robust mtDNA analysis even from a single cell.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial copy number in cells.

claim: For mtDNA mutation 3082, a mixture of both homoplasmic and heteroplasmic models is in action.
source: For four mtDNA variants (VAF between 0.5% ~ 24% at population level), we find that a mixture of both models is in action for different variants (Figure 1E). For instance, mtDNA mutation 3082 is widely spread among single cells, but at low frequency per cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: It is extremely unlikely that the identical mutation arose independently in every single cell.
source: Because it is extremely unlikely (see Materials and method) that the identical mutation arose independently in every single cell, cells sharing the same mitochondrial mutations are inferred to have descended from the same ancestral cell.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical inference detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Cells sharing the same mitochondrial mutations are inferred to have descended from the same ancestral cell.
source: Because it is extremely unlikely (see Materials and method) that the identical mutation arose independently in every single cell, cells sharing the same mitochondrial mutations are inferred to have descended from the same ancestral cell.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical inference and is a key principle of the lineage tracing method.

claim: Even low frequency heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations can be exploited for lineage tracing.
source: These results suggest that even low frequency heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations can be exploited for lineage tracing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the single-cell data showing detection of low-frequency mutations.

claim: A hematopoietic stem cell first acquires an initiating mutation in one of a number of chromatin modifier genes in human AML.
source: Human AML is organized as a hierarchy: a hematopoietic stem cell first acquires an initiating mutation in one of a number of chromatin modifier genes, previously termed as 'pre-leukemic' hematopoietic stem cell (pHSC) (Jan et al., 2012; Corces-Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on AML biology.

claim: pHSCs are functionally normal and are not able to transplant AML.
source: pHSCs are functionally normal and are not able to transplant AML, but upon accumulation of additional mutations, they give rise to leukemic stem cells (LSCs) that are able to self-renew and recapitulate AML disease upon transplantation (Jan et al., 2012; Thomas and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on AML biology.

claim: pHSCs give rise to leukemic stem cells (LSCs) upon accumulation of additional mutations.
source: pHSCs are functionally normal and are not able to transplant AML, but upon accumulation of additional mutations, they give rise to leukemic stem cells (LSCs) that are able to self-renew and recapitulate AML disease upon transplantation (Jan et al., 2012; Thomas and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on AML biology.

claim: LSCs are able to self-renew and recapitulate AML disease upon transplantation.
source: pHSCs are functionally normal and are not able to transplant AML, but upon accumulation of additional mutations, they give rise to leukemic stem cells (LSCs) that are able to self-renew and recapitulate AML disease upon transplantation (Jan et al., 2012; Thomas and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on AML biology.

claim: LSCs give rise to the bulk leukemic blast cells in AML.
source: Finally, LSCs give rise to the bulk leukemic blast cells in AML (Thomas and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on AML biology.

claim: Targeted exome sequencing in AML samples have identified somatic mutations in tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes that link the lineage relationship of pHSCs, LSCs and blasts.
source: Targeted exome sequencing in these samples have identified somatic mutations in tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes that link the lineage relationship of pHSCs, LSCs and blasts, providing the ground truth for our analyses (Corces-Zimmerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work that provides validation for the current study.

claim: The LSC and blast populations not only shared the same heteroplasmic variants, but also showed similar distribution and allele frequency at the cellular level.
source: Using high-confidence mtDNA mutations, detected both from bulk ATAC-seq and single cell ATAC-seq, we found the LSC and blast populations not only shared the same heteroplasmic variants, but also showed similar distribution and allele frequency at the cellular level (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: LSC and blast populations are identical at the genetic level, but divergent at the epigenomic level.
source: These results indicate the two populations are identical at the genetic level, but divergent at the epigenomic level, consistent with previous studies (Corces et al., 2016; Schep et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mtDNA data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Four diagnostic mtDNA mutations were identified in the same cell in patient SU353.
source: In patient SU353, we identified four diagnostic mtDNA mutations in the same cell (Figure 1F), which indicates these four mitochondrial variants already co-existed in the ancestral cell (see Materials and method).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When a single variant allele has a frequency greater than 20%, the detection rate can be up to 90% with >20X coverage.
source: We found that when a single variant allele has a frequency greater than 20%, the detection rate can be up to 90% with >20X coverage (e.g. site 6776).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: When the variant allele has a frequency lower than 1%, the detection rate drops to 20% when the coverage is below 100X.
source: In contrast, when the variant allele has a frequency lower than 1%, the detection rate drops to 20% when the coverage is below 100X (e.g. site 6705).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: With any combination of the four variants, 90% (sensitivity) of the cells can be unambiguously assigned to the correct lineage with just 20x mtDNA coverage.
source: With any combination of the four variants, 90% (sensitivity) of the cells can be unambiguously assigned to the correct lineage with just 20x mtDNA coverage (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Two mtDNA mutations identified in pHSCs were never detected (false positive = 0) in LSCs and blasts.
source: Furthermore, two mtDNA mutations identified in other cells (e.g. pHSC specific site 2967,6268) were never detected (false positive = 0) in LSCs and blasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing a high specificity of the method.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Somatic DNA mutations in the mitochondrial genome are a powerful endogenous marker to identify clonal cell populations.
source: These results demonstrate that somatic DNA mutations in the mitochondrial genome are a powerful endogenous marker to identify clonal cell populations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing high sensitivity and specificity.

claim: Heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations were identified in multiple cell populations of primary blood cells from healthy donors and all AML patients.
source: We identified heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations in multiple cell populations of primary blood cells from healthy donors and all AML patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations showed a similar mutant spectrum as observed by previous studies using cancer genomic data.
source: The heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations showed a similar mutant spectrum as observed by previous studies using cancer genomic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C) (Ju et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C and citation to prior work.

claim: EMBLEM confirmed the previous lineage hierarchy of AML.
source: Furthermore, EMBLEM, not only confirmed the previous lineage hierarchy of AML, but also extended the previous model of pHSC heterogeneity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript that is consistent with prior models.

claim: EMBLEM extended the previous model of pHSC heterogeneity.
source: Furthermore, EMBLEM, not only confirmed the previous lineage hierarchy of AML, but also extended the previous model of pHSC heterogeneity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the discovery of pHSC-specific mtDNA mutations indicating subclonal heterogeneity.

claim: The LSCs and their corresponding leukemic blasts have nearly identical heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations.
source: In the AML cases with LSCs sequenced by ATAC-seq, the LSCs and their corresponding leukemic blasts have nearly identical heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting a direct lineage relationship and short generation history between LSCs and blasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is a direct lineage relationship and short generation history between LSCs and blasts.
source: In the AML cases with LSCs sequenced by ATAC-seq, the LSCs and their corresponding leukemic blasts have nearly identical heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting a direct lineage relationship and short generation history between LSCs and blasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of nearly identical mtDNA mutations between LSCs and blasts.

claim: Blast-associated mtDNA mutations were detected in pHSCs in all 11 cases.
source: We detected blast-associated mtDNA mutations in pHSCs in all 11 cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 11 AML patient samples.

claim: Additional heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations present specifically in pHSCs were detected.
source: Interestingly, we also detected additional heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations present specifically in pHSCs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Seven out of 11 cases have pHSC-unique heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations.
source: In the 11 cases we investigated, seven cases have pHSC-unique heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), a previously unrecognized level of pHSC heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: pHSC-unique heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations represent a previously unrecognized level of pHSC heterogeneity.
source: In the 11 cases we investigated, seven cases have pHSC-unique heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), a previously unrecognized level of pHSC heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the novel discovery of pHSC-specific mutations.

claim: pHSCs are capable of long-term self-renewal and possess a clonal growth advantage.
source: pHSCs are capable of long-term self-renewal and possess a clonal growth advantage, allowing them to clonally outcompete normal HSCs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about pHSC biology.

claim: The clonal frequency of pHSCs is a poor prognostic factor for overall survival in AML.
source: Indeed, the clonal frequency of pHSCs is a poor prognostic factor for overall survival in AML (Corces et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The discovery of pHSCs with distinct heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations suggests the existence of multiple distinct sub-clones of pHSCs in AML patients.
source: Our discovery of pHSCs with distinct heteroplasmic mtDNA mutations suggests the existence of multiple distinct sub-clones of pHSCs in AML patients.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of distinct mtDNA mutations in pHSCs.

claim: Single-cell ATAC-seq of HSCs from AML patient SU353 separated the HSCs into three lineages: Two clonal subpopulations termed 'clone 1' (18 cells) and 'clone 2' (104 cells), and a third population with no mtDNA variants (31 cells).
source: We identified the heteroplasmic mtDNA variants from each single cell, which separated the HSCs into three lineages: Two clonal subpopulations termed 'clone 1' (18 cells) and 'clone 2' (104 cells), and a third population with no mtDNA variants despite sufficient mtDNA coverage (pHSC with WT mtDNA, 31 cells) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Clone 2 possessed pHSC-specific mtDNA mutations, while clone 1 possessed mtDNA mutations shared with LSCs.
source: Notably, clone 2 possessed pHSC-specific mtDNA mutations, while clone 1 possessed mtDNA mutations shared with LSCs, indicating clone1 is the lineage precursor of AML.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell mtDNA mutation data.

claim: Clone 1 is the lineage precursor of AML.
source: Notably, clone 2 possessed pHSC-specific mtDNA mutations, while clone 1 possessed mtDNA mutations shared with LSCs, indicating clone1 is the lineage precursor of AML.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that clone 1 shares mutations with LSCs.

claim: Multiple pHSC clones arise in AML patients, and one subclone eventually evolved to become the LSC.
source: These results confirm that multiple pHSC clones arise in AML patients, and one subclone eventually evolved to become the LSC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the single-cell lineage tracing data.

claim: The chromatin accessibility profiles of pHSCs are more similar to HSCs than to LSCs or leukemic blasts.
source: The chromatin accessibility profiles of pHSCs are more similar to HSCs than to LSCs or leukemic blasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The greatest deviation between HSC and other cell types occurred at DNA binding motifs of the transcription factor Jun/Fos.
source: The greatest deviation between HSC and other cell types occurred at DNA binding motifs of the transcription factor Jun/Fos, a known key regulator of HSC biology (Santaguida et al., 2009) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2F and citation to prior work.

claim: Jun/Fos is a known key regulator of HSC biology.
source: The greatest deviation between HSC and other cell types occurred at DNA binding motifs of the transcription factor Jun/Fos, a known key regulator of HSC biology (Santaguida et al., 2009) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The three lineages of pHSCs revealed by mtDNA mutations showed distinctive chromatin profiles.
source: Furthermore, the three lineages of pHSCs revealed by mtDNA mutations also showed distinctive chromatin profiles (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Clone 1 pHSC, which gives rise to the LSC and AML leukemia, is already more similar to LSCs and blasts in its chromatin accessibility.
source: Clone 1 pHSC, which gives rise to the LSC and AML leukemia, is already more similar to LSCs and blasts in its chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis comparing different clones.

claim: Clone 2 that comprises the larger fraction of pHSCs exhibited variable chromatin profiles at the single-cell level that spanned the range of normal HSCs.
source: In contrast, clone 2 that comprises the larger fraction of pHSCs exhibited variable chromatin profiles at the single-cell level that spanned the range of normal HSCs, pHSC with WT mtDNA(WT cells), is also diverged from normal HSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis of clone 2.

claim: Both lineage tracing and single cell epigenomic states indicate clone 1 as the original stem cell of the AML in patient SU353.
source: Thus, both lineage tracing and single cell epigenomic states indicate clone 1 as the original stem cell of the AML in patient SU353.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined lineage and epigenomic data.

claim: Supervised comparison of the chromatin accessibility profiles among clonal sub-populations identified distinct and significantly enriched transcription factor motifs.
source: Supervised comparison of the chromatin accessibility profiles among these clonal sub-populations further identified distinct and significantly enriched transcription factor motifs (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The heterogeneity of HSCs from AML patients exists both on a genetic and epigenomic level.
source: These results indicate the heterogeneity of HSCs from AML patients both on a genetic and epigenomic level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined genetic and epigenomic data.

claim: EMBLEM is applicable to any eukaryote.
source: This approach is applicable to any eukaryote, does not require genetic engineering or genome editing, and is cost effective as the lineage information comes 'for free' on top of epigenomic insights.
evidence: This claim is based on the fact that all eukaryotes have mitochondria with mtDNA.

claim: EMBLEM does not require genetic engineering or genome editing.
source: This approach is applicable to any eukaryote, does not require genetic engineering or genome editing, and is cost effective as the lineage information comes 'for free' on top of epigenomic insights.
evidence: This is a key feature of the method as it uses endogenous mutations.

claim: EMBLEM is cost effective as the lineage information comes 'for free' on top of epigenomic insights.
source: This approach is applicable to any eukaryote, does not require genetic engineering or genome editing, and is cost effective as the lineage information comes 'for free' on top of epigenomic insights.
evidence: This claim is based on the fact that mtDNA is already sequenced in ATAC-seq data.

claim: EMBLEM enables clonotype tracing in existing ATAC-seq data sets.
source: An important advantage of EMBLEM is that we enable clonotype tracing in existing ATAC-seq data sets and hierarchical lineage construction from ATAC-seq that thousands of labs have already generated.
evidence: This claim is based on the fact that the method can be applied to already-generated data.

claim: All future ATAC-seq data acquired for other inquiries will also have the benefit of lineage information.
source: All future ATAC-seq data acquired for other inquiries will also have the benefit of lineage information.
evidence: This claim is based on the fact that mtDNA is sequenced in all ATAC-seq experiments.

claim: EMBLEM may be extended to other single cell technologies, in which mtDNA is sequenced.
source: EMBLEM may also be extended to other single cell technologies, in which mtDNA is sequenced.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claim: EMBLEM is successful even with low frequency heteroplasmic mutations, detection of rare clones in a population, and authentic clinical samples.
source: We show that EMBLEM is successful even with low frequency heteroplasmic mutations, detection of rare clones in a population, and authentic clinical samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ludwig et al. (2019) reported the feasibility of using mtDNA and single cell genomics for lineage tracing.
source: During revision of this work, Ludwig et al. (2019) reported the feasibility of using mtDNA and single cell genomics for lineage tracing, which independently validates the potentially broad utility of this approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to concurrent work.

claim: One limitation of EMBLEM is absence of mtDNA mutations in cells and tissues of embryos and young animals.
source: One limitation of this method is absence of mtDNA mutations in cells and tissues of embryos and young animals, which precluded us from applying EMBLEM to published scATAC-seq data of early animal development.
evidence: This is a stated limitation based on the biology of mtDNA mutation accumulation.

claim: The possibility of selective mitochondrial inheritance or intercellular mitochondria transfer may affect the accuracy of inferred lineages.
source: Moreover, the possibility of selective mitochondrial inheritance or intercellular mitochondria transfer may affect the accuracy of inferred lineages (Mishra and Chan, 2014; Moschoi et al., 2016; Marlein et al., 2017; Hayakawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a stated limitation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Asymmetric transmission of mitochondria would not necessarily affect cellular lineage tracing, as long as the variant alleles are randomly segregated.
source: On the other hand, asymmetric transmission of mitochondria would not necessarily affect cellular lineage tracing, as long as the variant alleles are randomly segregated.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration about the method's robustness.

claim: Species-specific mtDNA always paired with species-specific nuclear genomic DNA in a human-mouse mixing experiment.
source: Using scATAC-seq data from a mixing experiment with human and mouse cells (Satpathy et al., 2018), we found species-specific mtDNA always paired with species-specific nuclear genomic DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a mixing experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mitochondrial horizontal transfer is not a confounder of this study and does not universally occur between cells.
source: These results suggest that mitochondrial horizontal transfer is not a confounder of our study and does not universally occur between cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the species-mixing experiment results.

claim: The pHSC population is heterogeneous, with evidence of multiple mtDNA clones.
source: mtDNA lineage tracing produced new insights concerning the pHSC, the human hematopoietic stem cell that suffers the first oncogenic mutation in AML evolution. Our results add to the evidence that the pHSC population is heterogeneous, with evidence of multiple mtDNA clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by the discovery of multiple distinct mtDNA clones in pHSCs.

claim: The pHSC lineage that gives rise to the subsequent acute myeloid leukemia is not the lineage with the best competitive potential among pHSCs.
source: Unexpectedly, the pHSC lineage that gives rise to the subsequent acute myeloid leukemia is not the lineage with the best competitive potential among pHSCs, as the leukemogenic lineage is often in the minority.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that clone 1, which gives rise to AML, is smaller than clone 2.

claim: pHSC burden is a strong poor prognostic predictor of AML survival.
source: pHSC burden is a strong poor prognostic predictor of AML survival (Corces et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: High pHSC burden may reflect the diversity of pHSCs or the underlying mutational processes.
source: Our analysis suggests that high pHSC burden may reflect the diversity of pHSCs or the underlying mutational processes.
evidence: This is a new interpretation based on the findings of pHSC heterogeneity.

claim: 43M paired-end ATAC-seq reads (2 × 50 bp) yielded the same coverage of mtDNA as 747M paired-end reads (2 × 250 bp) from WGS-H data.
source: 43M paired-end ATAC-seq reads (2 × 50 bp) yielded the same coverage of mtDNA as 747M paired-end reads (2 × 250 bp) from WGS-H data.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: During DNA transposition and amplification in cells, mitochondrial DNA is also amplified at the same time.
source: During DNA transposition and amplification in cells, mitochondrial DNA is also amplified at the same time (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of what happens during the ATAC-seq protocol.

claim: High drop-out rate is a common challenge for single-cell technologies.
source: While high drop-out rate is a common challenge for single-cell technologies (Kharchenko et al., 2014), computational imputation of the missing information from single cell data can address this problem (Zhang and Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on single-cell technologies.

claim: Computational imputation of the missing information from single cell data can address the drop-out problem.
source: While high drop-out rate is a common challenge for single-cell technologies (Kharchenko et al., 2014), computational imputation of the missing information from single cell data can address this problem (Zhang and Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on computational methods.

claim: When multiple mtDNA variants are co-detected in multiple single cells, we can infer their origin and linkage in the ancestral cell.
source: When multiple mtDNA variants are co-detected in multiple single cells, we can infer their origin and linkage in the ancestral cell (see Materials and method).
evidence: This is a methodological principle of the lineage inference approach.

claim: Cells containing any one of the linked variants will still inform their origin from the same lineage.
source: Thus, cells containing any one of these variants will still inform their origin from the same lineage.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle of linked variants.
